# Copper August 2011 

- Just as the talk was returning copper back to the $10,000/t level, economic uncertainty in the shape of renewed sovereign debt fears in Europe, in addition to concerns over the US debt ceiling, sent copper crashing at the start of August.  Cash quotes declined by over $1,200/t from the end of July to the low for the month on 10<sup>th</sup> August before directionless trade ensued for the remainder of the month as prices bounced between $8,700/t and $9,000/t. 

- Prices will continue to be driven by economic news and related sentiment in the short term, while the direction of physical premia will likely be the first indicator of whether there has been any real impact to demand from the knock to confidence that the latest round of debt problems has caused.  While we still expect prices to increase in the final quarter, we have lowered our forecast to $9,700/t from $10,000/t previously as a result of the lower starting point that the latest bout of debt panic has caused. 

- We have made a number of changes to our demand forecasts since last month, with the net result that we now forecast global demand growth of 5.1% this year.  Although this change is in itself relatively modest, there have been more significant changes within this global number.  Of particular note, we have upgraded our estimate of Chinese demand to 9.2% from 5% previously, while we have downgraded both Western European and US demand prospects for this year, to 0.3% and 3% respectively. 

- Spot TC/RC sales to traders declined below $50/t & 5c/lb during August as strikes and stock drawdowns weighed. There are several factors supporting these lower numbers, including the effects of the force majeure declared by Escondida during recent industrial action at the mine that forced various smelters in Asia to cover the resultant shortfall, either from the spot market or through other suppliers advancing tonnage.  The other factor relates to the ongoing decline in what had been a large inventory of concentrates in China, which contributed to lower spot rates and has eroded the CSPT’s desired floor price for purchases by a further $10/t & 1c/lb to $90/t & 9c/lb this month.

Copper Monthly Update 

## Market Developments 

**Sell in May and then again in August** Just as the talk was returning copper back to the $10,000/t level, economic uncertainty in the shape of renewed sovereign debt fears in Europe, in addition to concerns over the US debt ceiling sent copper crashing at the start of August.  Cash quotes declined by over $1,200/t from the end of July to the low for the month on 10<sup>th</sup> August before directionless trade ensued for the remainder of the month as prices bounced between $8,700/t and $9,000/t. 

**Debt deals didn’t dampen demand doubt driven declines** The price declines in the first few days of the month were relatively gentle, despite concerns over the potential for a US debt default as US lawmakers wrangled over raising their debt ceiling.  That Democrats and Republicans managed to agree a deal to lift the borrowing limit did little to boost prices however, which lurched sharply lower after a rating agency overlooked the deal and cut their assessment of US debt from its prior top notch.  At around the same time, fears that the European debt crisis would spread to Italy and Spain, in addition to France, all considered too big to fail, but significantly, too big to save, fanned fears that problems on both sides of the Atlantic would lead to a much talked about double-dip recession and consequently, weaker demand for industrial metals.  Meanwhile, the final pillar of support for current supply constraints was removed as workers at Chile’s Escondida agreed to go back to work after a two week stoppage, which left sentiment heavily weighed to the downside. 

**Prices range bound in second half of month** Prices rallied strongly on 11<sup>th</sup> August, bouncing back after touching the lowest level this year the prior day, with the focus moving to Chinese trade and currency news.  Initial Chinese trade data pointed to a further recovery in imports of copper, which was confirmed later in the month, while at the same time the People’s Bank of China fixed its exchange rate against the US dollar at a new record, which combined to lift the markets’ mood.  With the arbitrage window open for most of the month, in addition to the stronger domestic currency, this is supportive of our view of recovering Chinese imports through the remainder of the year.  Following on from this aforementioned bounce on 11<sup>th</sup> , prices were largely directionless, ebbing between $8,700/t and $9,000/t through the remainder of the month. 

**Threat of strike action looms large in the background** As we noted above, Escondida’s fortnight-long strike has ended but the threat of further disruptions elsewhere does loom large in the background, with workers at Collahuasi in Chile and at Freeport’s Grasberg mine in Indonesia poised to down tools.  The threat of a one day strike at Collahuasi on 2<sup>nd</sup> September relates to workers wanting colleagues who were fired after a previous disruption re-hired, while Freeport

Indonesia’s copper operations at Grasberg remain under threat of renewed strike action. This follows the failure of talks between the company and union representatives to reach an agreement to establish a new contract covering 2012-2013 once the one currently in force expires in October. The two sides are reportedly far apart on even the basic elements to typical contract talks, and the possibility of a sudden halt to operations looms large, although there has been no indication of when such action will begin. #### **Copper exchange stocks and cash LME price** 1800 10000

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - August 2011 Page 2 of 21 Copper Monthly Update **Stocks little changed through August** Exchange stock levels were little changed through the month overall, although Shanghai did edge slightly lower. The London Metal Exchange ended last month with inventories standing at 466,025 tonnes and remain at similar levels at the time or writing, with a pattern emerging of stocks edging slightly lower most days before a large shipment would break the declining streak. Stocks would then tick modestly lower again before a further large intake. On a regional basis, warehouses in Europe increased inventories but those in Asia and the US edged lower. It was a similar story for Comex stocks, which ended the month broadly where they began. In Shanghai, SHFE stocks finished the month down just under 15kt, to close August on 102.258kt, reversing at least part of the increase from last month, while bonded warehouse stock levels also declined by around 50kt through the month and now stand at around 300kt. Bonded warehouse stocks had increased by around 50kt the prior month, with part of the increase related to rising imports into China. #### **Shanghai/LME arbitrage ($/t) vs refined copper imports** Refined Imports cash arbitrage 3-month arbitrage

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - August 2011 Page 3 of 21 Copper Monthly Update **Chinese premia turn higher from month end slip** After slipping at the very end of the month, premia in China recovered to the $90-120/t range and point to firm demand conditions despite the usual seasonal slowdown. Indeed, that the front month SHFE contract moved into backwardation relative to three month copper confirmed this view. With the collapse in copper prices through August, scrap dealers became increasingly reluctant to sell material, resulting in scrap spreads tightening and direct use of scrap by semis producers declining. As such, semis plants increased consumption of refined material, with this going some way to explaining the relative tightness in the market that firm premia suggest. **European and US premia unmoved** In Europe and the US, premia barely changed this month, although little trade was conducted in any case with semis producers and traders in the middle of their summer holidays. The movement of premia in the coming month will be interesting to watch as this will be the first indication of semis producer sentiment after the latest bout of panic associated with the European debt crisis. There have been plenty of reports of downstream mills being cautious over the outlook and placing orders for only what they need and suggesting a further round of destocking. However, with copper prices still at relatively high levels, there was little incentive for fabricators to keep anything other than what they need in any case and ordering on a hand to mouth basis is, therefore, business as usual. **2011 global demand downgraded despite increase in China** We have made a number of changes to our demand forecasts since last month, with the net result that we now forecast global growth of 5.1% this year, compared to our previous forecast of 5.4%. Although this change in itself is relatively modest, there have been more significant changes within this global number. Of particular note, we have upgraded our estimate of Chinese demand to 9.2% from 5% previously, after detailed analyses of unreported stock changes. Meanwhile, we have downgraded both Western European and US demand prospects for this year, to growth of 0.3% and 3% respectively. **Lower starting point cuts Q4 price forecast** The l

ower estimate for 2011 consumption is, therefore, largely responsible for the change to our metal market balance, which now stands at a deficit of 351kt this year, compared to 408kt in July. Crucially, we still expect a deficit and the modest adjustment does not alter our view of fundamentally supported prices in the final part of the year. What has changed, however, is the starting point. At the time of writing prices hover just above $9,000/t after the collapse in the early part of August, and as a consequence we have a much lower starting point for prices to move from than was the case at the end of July when we wrote our last report. As such, while we still expect prices to increase in the final quarter, we have lowered our forecast to $9,700/t from $10,000/t previously, in addition to cutting our estimate of Q3 prices to $9,200/t. Our estimate of full year prices has also been reduced to $9,420/t, although we have maintained our forecast for 2012 at $9,588/t, with prices expected to peak in the second quarter in line with seasonal demand strength. Prices will continue to be driven by economic news and related sentiment in the short term, while the direction of physical premia will likely be the first indicator of whether there has been any real impact to demand from the knock to confidence that the latest round of debt problems has caused. #### **Price forecasts and world quarterly supply/demand balance – (kt)** |||**Refined**

Although this change in itself is relatively modest, there have been more significant changes within t

his global number. Of particular note, we have upgraded our estimate of Chinese demand to 9.2% from 5% previously following detailed analysis of unreported stock changes. Meanwhile, we have downgraded both Western European and US demand prospects for this year, to 0.3% and 3% respectively. ### **Europe and CIS** **Western European demand outlook downgraded** Although we do not have a full set of first half data, we have a pretty good feel for activity in the January to June period of 2011 and this has led us to downgrade demand across much of the region. Key changes include German growth being toned down from 4.9% to 3.6% this year, while for France and Spain our previous forecasts of positive growth this year have turned into expectations of full year contraction. Overall, these changes result in Western European demand being little more than flat this year, with consumption in 2012 improving in the region of 1%. **Industrial slowdown begins to pinch in June** Although these downgrades come against the backdrop of the ongoing European debt crisis, they are not directly related to it. We have always been of the view that industrial and economic activity will slow in the second half of the year but this perhaps came a little earlier than we anticipated. Indeed, eurozone industrial production fell by 0.7% month on month in June, well short of analyst expectations of an increase of 0.1%. The decline was due to a 2.5% drop in durable consumer goods, while capital goods and intermediate goods also suffered, slipping 1.5% and 0.6%, respectively. Output declined in both France and Germany. Year over year, eurozone industrial production rose by 2.9%, however. The data showed that for the full 27 EU states there was an even greater decline of 1.2% month on month, with year-on-year growth of just 1.7%. **Lead indicators point to further weakness** Lead indicators suggest that further monthly falls in IP should be expected through the third quarter as weakness in consumer demand persists. The preliminary eurozone PMI for August fell to 49.7 from 50.35, dipping below the 50 expansion threshold for the first time since September 2009, while the new orders index hit a 2-year low of 46.9. **Aurubis wire rod production slows in calendar Q2** The latest quarterly earnings results from cathode and semis producer Aurubis has revealed a decline in wire rod output of 5.7% year on year to 198kt in the second calendar quarter of the year. This was also lower than first quarter output of 217kt. However, softening the blow somewhat, production of copper shapes recovered from the first quarter dip to post a 10% year-on-year rise to 55kt. #### **Aurubis wire rod production – (kt)** 120 240

**Demand in seasonal lull** European Cathode demand in August has been relatively muted, with semis producers in the midst of work and maintenance shutdowns. More visibility into whether there has been any real impact from the ongoing debts crisis will emerge in the coming weeks, although the latest European IP and PMI data do suggest a slowdown in demand in the final part of the year. Metals Market Service Monthly Update - August 2011 Page 5 of 21 Copper Monthly Update **Russian authorities introduce variable export duty** A variable duty has been introduced on exports of copper cathode from Russia, with the duty set to increase as the copper price rises. Nothing will be payable on exports when the copper price is below $6,000/t, while a 10% duty will be applied when the price is in the range $6,000-$8,000/t. At prices above $8,000/t, $800 plus 30% of the price above $8,000 will be payable. This replaces the current rule where a 10% tax is levied on all cathode exports, which was reintroduced this year and has indirectly resulted in a sharp rise in Russian apparent consumption of copper. In a bid to avoid the export duty, firms are producing wire rod, thus increasing consumption, and exporting this instead of cathode. Russian exports of refined copper were down by 68% in the first half of the year at 75.167kt, while wire rod exports more than doubled to 178.435kt in the same period. We currently estimate apparent refined consumption growth of 57.4% to 700kt in 2011, although it must be noted that this simply puts Russian demand back on a par with 2008, the year before the previous cathode export tax was suspended. ### **Americas** **Mixed bag of macrodata not enough to outweigh usual summer decline in US** The seasonal slowdown across the northern hemisphere was pretty evident in the USA, with select data highlighting factory closures and holiday periods. Total vehicle production fell sharply in July from the previous month, but on a seasonally-adjusted annualised rate output was up by 10% m-o-m to 8.73 million units, just shy of the level reached in March before operations were disrupted by parts shortages. Total vehicle sales increased by 6% m-o-m in July (on a seasonally-adjusted basis) to 12.2M units, but this rate of sales is below the level of late 2010 and early 2011. The improvement over May and June suggests that easing fuel prices are tempting consumers back into the market, even for the bigger-ticket items such as large SUVs. US unemployment remains stubbornly high, and is likely to do so with government job losses reducing the impact of private-sector creation last month. Despite consumer confidence levels picking up a notch in July to 59.5, we would typically look for a reading of 90 to reflect a healthy state to the economy, so there is some way to go yet before we can satisfy this condition. On a better note, however,

US durable goods orders rose by 4% in July vs. the disappointing 2.1% contraction in June.  July’s rate benefited from high transportation equipment orders, with commercial aircraft doing particularly well. 

In the US housing market, starts fell by 1.5% m-o-m in July to an annual rate of 604,000, but were still up by 9.8% y-o-y. Building permits, which measure future building activity, fell by 3.2% m-o-m. It appears that housing starts are still struggling to gain momentum, especially with a decline in building permits.  Indeed, it is hard to imagine much of an improvement before the end of 2012.  To illustrate how far housing starts have to go, a healthy market would see these grow at an annual rate of approximately 1.2 million.  Meanwhile, existing-home sales fell 3.5% m-o-m in July to an annual rate of 4.67 million, an eight-month low.  Lawrence Yun, the National Association of Realtors’ chief economist, stated that although home prices are very favorable, buyers “…are being held back because banks are only offering financing to the most highly qualified borrowers.” 

**Rod markets reflect summer slowdown** At the metals level, rod production levels for July of 96.7kt confirm the downtrend that has been in place since May, according to data from the American Bureau of Metals Statistics.  Equally, ABMS data also show the commensurate decline in rod shipments, from 108kt to 95kt in July.  Shipments for the first seven months of this year were down by 2.1% compared to the same period for 2010, to 744kt.  Meanwhile, revised data from the Copper and Brass Servicecenter Association show that distributors’ shipments to June have also stalled. During this first half, the CBSA’s members shipped an average of 10.2kt/m, no better than H1 2010.  The one upside is that some players believe that poor sales to the depressed construction sector are finally hitting bottom and stabilising, rather than showing potential for worsening.  Even so, we have taken the precaution of reducing our forecast copper demand for the USA this year slightly, to 1.813Mt from 1.841Mt, due to the weaker rod environment. 

**Russian rod makes appearance in US market** For the first time since March 2009, the USA became a net importer of copper rod in June, thanks largely to an unexpected influx of rod from Russia.  We had previously reported that Russian _cathode_ exports would shrink owing to the new export tax on the product from last December, and through to May most of the rod – having been converted from cathode by domestic producers to avoid the duty – had shown up in Europe, mainly in Turkey.  But if US rod markets were looking flat since May, no one told the Russians about it, and in May the first batch of imports from Russia (c.400t) since January 2009 showed up into the US ports of New Orleans and Baltimore.  This ballooned into 6.7kt in June, and is likely to stem US optimism for better rod prices as we head into the Q3 ordering period.  In the past, Russian material h

as come into the US market rather sporadically, but the additional export tax on cathode issued this month is likely to maintain cathode-to-rod conversion at home for some time, and hence higher than normal rod exports from Russia might well become more established for the rest of this year. Besides this Russian material, the formerly bankrupt Sherburne Metals copper rod mill in upstate NY should be recommissioned during October with the assistance of UpCast staff, and is likely to be active selling its own rod into the market by late-Q4. This re-activation should add c.30kt capacity; the second line (15kt/a) is unlikely to receive attention from UpCast technical personnel as it was not an official UpCast line. ### **China** **Inflation prospects recede despite recent jump in prices** The recent trend of accelerating price inflation yet slowing industrial activity has continued into the latest available Chinese data set for July. Consumer prices increased slightly in July and rocketing food prices are an ongoing source of discontent. However, we do think that inflation is peaking in China and should begin to slow in the fourth quarter. Meanwhile, industrial production rose by 14.0% year on year in July, slower than the 15.1% growth recorded in June but on par with growth through the first half. Heavy industry rose by 14.5%, while light industry expanded by 12.8%. IP growth was 0.9% in month-on-month terms. In contrast to 2008, the global slowdown is coming at a time when China is steaming ahead, and although Chinese export growth may slow it still does not seem likely that IP will be severely impacted. **Chinese growth prospects upgraded** A detailed review of first half data has led to an upgrade in our estimate of full year growth in China this year. Looking at apparent consumption statistics alone, without consideration of unreported stock movements, these fail to take into account the significant stock changes that typically take place in China through the year. Indeed, it is a much shallower stock build in China in the first quarter this year than took place in 2010 that has resulted in real demand rising by 7.3% in Q1 by our estimates. When stripping out stock movements this would have been a contraction of around 6% in the same period. This was also a feature of second quarter demand data, with real demand estimated to have grown by some 13.8%, compared to a simple apparent consumption calculation which rev

eals an 8% contraction.  For the full year we now expect growth in refined copper consumption of 9.2% in 2011, slowing to 7% the following year. 

**Imports continue steady uptick** It is difficult to characterise the improvement of imports into China as anything other than steady; however, this still offers comfort to our full year forecast.  If anything, imports into China this year have been the major disappointment, although since May they have at least been improving.  Latest data for July revealed imports were still lower by some 14.5% on a year-on-year basis at 190.5kt but on an upward monthly trend, boosted by the SHFE/LME arbitrage window opening up in the preceding months.  After closing again over the last couple of months, the window has reopened as of late, pointing to continued improvement in the months to come.  That one of the measures China is using to fight inflation is to allow its currency to appreciate only favours our assessment of further gains in imports as foreign material becomes relatively less expensive.  The favourable arbitrage, in addition to sharp declines seen over the past month, have led to semis producers stocking up on cathode in August.  As a result, bonded warehouse stocks ebbed lower again in August by around 50kt and now stand at around 300kt after edging higher by a similar amount in the previous month. 

**Build up of wire rod stocks** Heading into August anecdotal evidence suggested that there was a build up of stocks of wire rod at mills and that despite this, firms have been maintaining output at relatively high levels.  There is no obvious reason why a company would continue to produce significantly ahead of order levels except in the very short term as amassing stocks of finished goods would simply increase working capital requirements and with copper prices so high, this does not make a lot of sense.  However, there may also be a difference between the state owned enterprises and the private sector in China in the sense that the SOE rod plants will be funded by local banks and will simply “spend” their budget allocations in terms of buying cathodes and produce whatever they can regardless of whether or not there is an immediate market for this wire rod.

It is also worth mentioning that the massive end-use growth rates seen in China over the past few years has meant that pipeline stocks of all intermediaries must have been substantial over an extended period of time.  Clearly, if end-use demand growth has tapered off then stocks of wire rod will certainly appear to be high relative to off-take.  Meanwhile, perhaps some firms were producing at high rates in anticipation of summer power outages, which led to a stock build.  In all likelihood, the real explanation is a combination of all of the above. 

**Affordable homes target cut for 2012** China has reportedly cut its target for the construction of affor

dable homes to be built next year to 8 million. Previously, plans were to build 36m affordable homes by 2015, including 10m this year and in 2012. On the face of it this should be negative for demand growth next year, but that said we do not expect this to cause any major downturn in consumption of copper from the sector. Indeed, construction activity has maintained a strong pace this year and given the lag between construction starts and copper use in buildings, this year’s strength will likely sustain copper demand well into next year. However, we maintain our previously stated view that the disconnect between housing starts and completions points to a slowdown in construction activity at some point. #### **Chinese production of copper semis – (kt)** 80 1100

### **Japan** **Industrial activity continues on recovery track** The Japanese industrial sector appears to be recovering at a faster pace than initially expected, with latest data for industrial output underscoring this point. In fact, IP rose by 3.8% month on month in June, marking the third consecutive monthly gain and with the transport sector providing much of the impetus. Meanwhile, a survey by the Ministry of Economics, Trade and Industry showed that a further 2.2% gain was expected in July, and 2% in August. The data suggest that production will return to pre-quake levels this autumn, much sooner than previously expected. **Japanese demand upgraded following stronger than expected Q2** In the wake of the disasters that struck Japan in March we had lowered our estimate of consumption in Japan for the full year. However, to our surprise, semis output maintained a firm pace through the April to June period as the construction of temporary homes boosted shipments, despite weakness in the transport and electronics sectors. As a result, we have upgraded our view of apparent demand for the full year in Japan to a contraction of 2%, compared to our previous estimate of decline of some 6%. **Shipments ease back in July** Wire and cable shipments ebbed lower in July, falling by 7.5% year on year while also slipping on the prior month. On a sectoral basis, construction disappointed, posting its first year-on-year fall in a year, while autos also registered a further fall on the year ago figure, however, the volume was the highest level since February. For the year to July, shipments were just negative, although on a brighter note, production of wire and cable has fared better this year. Indeed, production was up by 3.9% in the first half of the year, buoyed by stronger output of power cable. **Japanese vehicle output continue

s to recover…** June auto production decreased by 14% year on year, a vast improvement over the average decline of 50% in the preceding 3 months. Toyota recently commented that restoration has occurred at a faster-than-expected speed. It plans to hire up to 4000 contract workers in Japan to help make up for lost ground and output should have fully recovered by September. Toyota estimates the quake will reduce annual output by 150,000 units, down by 2/3rds from its previous estimates. **China’s 7M 2011 concentrate imports down by 10.7% on a year earlier** According to official customs statistics, Chinese copper concentrate imports were 452.6kdmt in July, which represents a decline of 3.7% on the same month last year.  Moreover, on a cumulative basis through the first seven months of 2011, the country’s overall receipts remained suppressed relative to last year, being lower by 10.7% at 3.4Mdmt.  Chile’s contribution remained significantly less (-29.7%) than in 2010 due to lower output at Escondida, port problems at Collahuasi etc.  Turkey also recorded a sizeable reduction in shipments (-61.1%) in part due to the reactivation of the 30kt/a Samsun facility.  The owners of this plant have also installed a dedicated copper refinery (previously the smelter’s blister output was sold to traders). 

**Ramp up of new Chinese smelting capacity should result in higher concentrate imports** Earlier we mentioned declining concentrate stockpiles in China as being a contributor to falling spot TC/RCs.  There are a number of reasons for this.  Firstly, the 200kt/a Kunming smelter belonging to Yunnan Copper was re-started in February 2010 after having been out of operation for 231 days (41 days less than anticipated).  The official reason for the closure was to fu

lly overhaul the IsaSmelt furnace and ancillary equipment; however, some market commentators believed that another reason for the long shutdown was due to depressed TC/RCs.  Elsewhere, Daye commissioned its new Ausmelt furnace, which has a greater capacity than the previous configuration.  More recently, in Q2 2011 the capacity of the Xiangguang smelter in Shandong province was doubled from 200kt/a to 400kt/a.  Elsewhere, a number of projects have been ramping up production this year, including the 100kt/a Tianzhong plant in Yunnan, which has replaced an old 35kt/a blast furnace operation, Hengbang in Sichuan province (50kt/a), Houma in Shanxi province (+50kt/a), Kunpeng in Sichuan province (100kt/a) and Yunnan Tin in Yunnan province (100kt/a).  Finally, Zijin Mining’s 200kt/a smelter in Fujian province is expected to be commissioned during the latter stages of Q4. 

**Chinese raw materials stocks built up in 2010 have now halved** Below is an update of an analysis of raw material stock movements based upon official CNIA data.  This shows the make-up of refined production from primary and secondary sources.  We have removed imported blister from the CNIA secondary production data as this appears to be included in these statistics.  We have then compared the primary refined production figures with the various components that make up this number, i.e. from domestic and imported concentrates, SxEw and imported blister and matte.  Note that these figures are shown on a recoverable basis (i.e. net of 3.4% overall smelting losses where appropriate).  This comparison allows us to calculate an implied stock change for each year.  What this shows is that there has been an implied stock drawdown in each year from 2007 to 2009 and a modest stock build in 2010.  A drawdown of this magnitude (the implied cumulative stock build during the three years to 2009 is 458kt Cu) is not realistic, nor is the very modest stock build in 2010.  If we take the average stock drawdown between 2007 and 2009 plus an allowance for maintaining normal stocks in this growing market and express these as a percentage of the average refined production over the same period we might infer that the statistics are missing the equivalent of 4.5% of refined production in terms of raw material feed in each year.  This missing feed is most likely to be from secondary sources, such as unreported scrap, and domestically-produced reverts and by-products from zinc, lead and nickel smelting (cakes, speiss, matte, dross etc.) If we then apply this unreported feed factor (4.5% of refined production) this allows us to determine a more plausible stock change for each year.

**Further stock depletion will cut China’s influence on spot TC/RCs** This updated analysis implies that, of the 259kt of stocks accumulated during 2010, approximately 50% of this tonnage was drawn down during the first seven months of 2011.  This estimate appears reasonable in relation to the anecdotal evidence that we have gleaned.  What this also tells us is that unless China raises its monthly imports of copper concentrates over the balance of this year (i.e. in order to satisfy rising smelter demand) then it will have to draw down these stocks much further (or cut output).  In this manner Chinese smelters risk losing or eroding what has been a major competitive edge in being able to effectively dictate the level of spot terms in the international concentrates market.  Such an outcome will, no doubt, have a bearing on longterm TC/RC negotiations in the forthcoming Mating Season, because long-term rates have a tendency to be influenced by prevailing spot terms.

**Forecast refined output dropped by 65kt** Since our last report we have dropped our forecast 2011 refined copper production capability by 65kt, with the main reductions coming in Latin America (-56kt) and Asia (-33kt) being only partially offset by increments from the former East Bloc region (+10kt) and Europe (+9kt), although net of adjustments the overall reduction is just 5kt. **Codelco commercial copper output up barely 1% in H1 2011** Codelco recorded a mere 0.9% year-on-year increase in its H1 2011 commercial copper output, rising from 837.7kt to 843.6kt (including the company’s 49% stake in El Abra). This brings into question the possibility of reaching the most recent 2011 production target of 1.7Mt.  Codelco Norte produced 436.1kt ( _vs_ 439.6kt in 2010), Salvador 34.9kt (35.6kt), Andina 55.9kt (41.9kt), El Teniente 181.6kt (188.2kt), Gabriela Mistral 52.5kt (58.8kt) and El Abra 25.4kt (37.2kt).  Note that these figures are not the company’s mine production, but the sum of the various products that each division produces (cathodes, blister and metal in concentrates). While some of the poorer performances reflect inclement weather and technical problems other issues, such as labour disputes, have also contributed.  This year we have seen a rash of unrest from contract workers at Codelco sites (many of whom were prior direct employees of the state-owned entity).  However, looking towards the rest of this year and probably into 2012, this particular issue may not be as prominent given the late-August agreement between contracting companies and their employees, which ensures bonus payment

s, presumably if certain conditions are met. 

Overall, Chilean copper output for H1 was down by 2.2%, to 2.571Mt as heavy rains and technical issues at various mines and associated mills took almost 150kt copper out of Q1 targets this year.  Xstrata Copper’s Collahuasi was one of the mines most affected by the inclement weather as well as previously reported port issues, as output fell by 12.1% during H1 2011 year on year to 234.5kt from 266.7kt.  Equally, Teck’s Quebrada Blanca also suffered from the rains, and produced 27% less copper during H1 (32.1kt _vs_ 44kt during the same period 2010).  Output at BHPB’s Minera Escondida, meanwhile, fell by over 14% to 450.7kt from 526kt, primarily due to technical problems affecting a conveyor belt and SAG mill during the first quarter.  On the other hand, better performances came from Candelaria (up by almost 33% during H1 to 71kt) and from the small mines sector (up by 31.5%, to 220.2kt).
